new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (no catalog record, existing_statements empty). The open pages give only a tone statement (three level tones, heavy functional load) and are silent on stress; consistent with the held Wilson 2003 dissertation (sec. 3.2.1, printed pp. 62-63: three phonemic tone levels H/M/L, no stress mention) and Blench 2011 Ce dictionary draft sec. 3.3 (tones). The deciding chapters 3 'Phoneme inventory' and 4 'Syllable structure' of the 1996 thesis were not readable.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the pages open to view Wilson treats Kuche as a tone language with three level tones (high, mid, low; rising/falling contours written over vowel sequences or with hachek/caret) and contrastive vowel length, both carrying a heavy functional load; tone is part of the phoneme inventory (chapter 3). Nothing in the visible pages (front matter, abstract, chapter 1) mentions stress, accent or prominence; the abstract summarises the phonology as open syllables, nasalized vowels surfacing as nasal codas and two vowel-harmony systems, with no stress statement. Whether chapters 3-4 (pp. 37-97, behind the ProQuest wall) say anything about stress remains unknown.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned in the visible pages
new_statements.identity_note: Kuche (autonym of the language of the Bache people; Hausa exonym Rukuba; Ethnologue/Glottolog 'Che'), spoken in at least 17 villages north-west of Jos, Plateau State, Nigeria; principal consultant Ruth Adiwu of Zagun (Kakek), with Gideon Asukutuk (Kisayhip) and Isaiah Ayhok (Jos); Wilson notes dialect differences between villages but describes one variety based mainly on Adiwu's speech and a 2,000-word list.

sources.note: The only full phonological description of the language; the source behind PHOIBLE's Che inventory (three level tones) and behind Blench's vowel/consonant analysis. A 186-page phonological grammar almost certainly has a suprasegmentals chapter that would settle whether any stress/prominence is described alongside tone.

sources.note: Catalog has no records for chee1238, so nothing to agree with or contradict; the work is silent on stress and supports treating Che as a tone language. It is the same author and language as the listed 1996 thesis and cites that thesis as one of the sources for the three-tone analysis. Chapters 4-8 and appendices (texts, tables) were not scanned; a stress statement there is very unlikely given the phonology sketch is in 3.2.1.

sources.note: §2 'Vowels, vowel harmony, and syllable structure in Kuche' (pp. 156-157): tense/lax vowel harmony, most syllables CV, CVC word-internally with nasal coda and word-finally; examples are tone-marked (low-tone vs mid-tone a- prefixes, 'not all phonological processes involving tone have been fully analyzed as yet', p. 165). Nothing on stress or accent. Cites Wilson 1996 as 'Ann Arbor, Michigan: University Microfilms, Inc.'
